title: Let The People Set The Pace Of Frontier AI | NOEMA
gist: Frontier AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI) and Musk have publicly converged on wanting to slow AI development, but the authors argue this is a nested 'stag hunt' collective-action problem that only a credible, independent witness can solve; they propose a standing 1,000-person Global Citizens' Assembly on AI, chosen by lot, with a legal 'duty to answer' enforceable via the EU AI Office.

insights.claim: On Sept. 12, 2026, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for easing the pace of AI model improvement and committed Anthropic to giving independent third-party evaluators ongoing, employee-like access to its systems; within hours OpenAI's Sam Altman agreed 'we need to pace the frontier' and made the same evaluator pledge, and Elon Musk responded with 'Dario is right.'
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Rare same-day public alignment across rival frontier labs on slowing capability gains and accepting outside evaluators is a concrete, checkable commitment investors and policymakers can track for follow-through or reversal.
insights.locator: On Sept. 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for an easing

insights.claim: Even with CEOs publicly agreeing to slow down, the authors argue the race will not actually stop because no single lab or government can unilaterally deliver restraint given the structural incentives each faces.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Public pacing pledges from labs should not be read as a de facto ceasefire in the capability race; expect continued frontier progress absent an external enforcement/verification mechanism.
insights.quote: But even if the CEOs agree, the race does not stop.
insights.locator: But even if the CEOs agree, the race does not stop.

insights.claim: More than 1,300 employees at leading AI companies have publicly called on Washington to back an international AI slowdown, signaling significant internal dissent inside frontier labs over catastrophic and extinction-level risk.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Internal labor unrest at scale is a leading indicator of governance/safety friction that could affect talent retention and regulatory posture at major AI labs.
insights.locator: researchers have left frontier labs amid disagreements over catastrophic

themes.theme: Nested collective-action problem, framed as a stag hunt

insights.claim: The authors frame the AI race not as a prisoner's dilemma (where defection always dominates) but as a Rousseauian 'stag hunt,' meaning a stable cooperative equilibrium (a paced, safe frontier) exists and is achievable if labs and governments can trust each other to hold the line, rather than requiring a global regulatory leviathan.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: This reframes the AI arms race as solvable via credible assurance mechanisms rather than as an inevitable race-to-the-bottom, changing the policy prescription from heavy-handed global regulation to trust-building infrastructure.
insights.quote: Instead, both collective-action problems look more like what game theorists call a “stag hunt,” after a parable of Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s.
insights.locator: What we are facing, in other words, is a double collective-action problem

insights.claim: The domestic race among AI labs and the geopolitical US-China race are causally nested: the argument 'if we slow down, China wins' is what American labs and officials use to block binding regulation, so ending the global (outer) race removes the domestic (inner) race's justification.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Any US-China AI coordination mechanism (even informal) could have outsized downstream effect on domestic US AI regulation by removing labs' primary anti-regulation argument.
insights.quote: The outer race is the inner one’s best excuse; end the global race, and the domestic one loses cover.
insights.locator: The two are linked: “If we slow down, China wins”

insights.claim: Evaluators engaged directly by the labs, and judged against risk thresholds the labs themselves define, cannot provide credible assurance to a rival lab or rival government; evidence only changes what competitors believe about each other's restraint when it flows through a party none of them controls.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Lab-selected 'independent' evaluator programs (as pledged by Anthropic/OpenAI) should be discounted by investors and regulators as trust-building signals unless evaluator selection and standards are externalized.
insights.locator: But evaluators engaged by the labs, judging against risk thresholds

insights.claim: The UN is disqualified as the credible global witness for AI pacing because the Security Council gives both Washington and Beijing a veto over the body meant to referee their rivalry, and because the UN is structurally an assembly of sovereign states rather than a body that can weigh humanity's interest above sovereignty.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Investors betting on UN-led AI governance frameworks as the coordination mechanism should discount that path; the authors argue it is structurally compromised by the very powers it would need to constrain.
insights.quote: It is an assembly of sovereigns, not a body that can stand above sovereignty and weigh it against humanity’s interests.
insights.locator: The obvious candidate is the United Nations

themes.theme: The Global Citizens' Assembly on AI proposal

insights.claim: The authors propose a standing Global Citizens' Assembly on AI of 1,000 people chosen by lot worldwide, sitting continuously (not producing a single report), with members serving fixed part-time terms and a third of seats regularly redrawn by lot, funded through an independent civic secretariat that pools disclosed funding from participating governments and labs without letting funders influence recruitment or evidence.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: This is the paper's core actionable policy proposal; watch for pilot funding from governments/foundations as the first concrete signal of traction.
insights.locator: Our proposal is a standing global citizens’ assembly of 1,000 people

insights.claim: The assembly's enforcement mechanism is a 'duty to answer': each recommendation would go to a named institution (a lab or government) with a fixed public deadline to state what it accepts, what it rejects, and why, with any published refusal open to public challenge.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: This is a soft-law accountability mechanism (public reputational pressure, not binding regulation) that could still move corporate behavior if adopted, especially if anchored in EU law.
insights.quote: Each recommendation from the assembly would go to a named institution, such as a lab or government, with a deadline to respond in public: what it accepts, what it rejects and why.
insights.locator: The duty to answer, in particular, is the key.

insights.claim: The assembly's size (1,000 members) is deliberately larger than statistically necessary for demographic representativeness; the authors argue the scale itself confers symbolic and political salience, making the body impossible for a lab CEO to dismiss the way they could dismiss a small expert panel.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Design choice signals the proposal is optimized for public/political leverage over corporations, not just statistical accuracy, which matters for assessing its likely real-world influence.
insights.quote: A CEO can shrug off a critic, even a panel of experts.
insights.locator: Why 1,000 global citizens? Is this not unwieldy?

themes.theme: EU AI Office as the nearest enforcement lever

insights.claim: Since August 2026, the EU's AI Office has had the power to fine a frontier-model provider or order mitigations or a recall, and Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI have all signed the safety and security chapter of its code of practice.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: The EU AI Office is currently the only body with live enforcement teeth (fines, mitigation orders, recalls) over all four major frontier labs, making it the most concrete existing regulatory chokepoint to monitor.
insights.quote: Since August, the EU’s AI Office can fine a frontier-model provider or order mitigations or a recall.
insights.locator: One jurisdiction already has enforcement powers of this kind.

insights.claim: Under the current EU code of practice, each lab defines its own risk tiers, judges for itself whether risks are acceptable, and picks its own outside evaluators, while public consultation ranks last among eight information-gathering methods and is used only 'if and insofar as necessary' -- meaning the most developed binding AI safety regime still treats the public as an input, not a party; the authors propose a clause obliging signatories to publicly answer a global assembly's recommendations as a fix.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Self-graded risk assessment under the EU's flagship AI safety regime is a real regulatory-arbitrage/greenwashing risk investors should price into 'compliance' claims by labs currently signed on.
insights.quote: Public consultation comes last among eight ways a lab may gather information, after web searches and market analyses.
insights.locator: But in this system, each lab reports to the regulator in full

insights.claim: The Chinese Communist Party has denounced Western-led 'exclusive groups' in AI governance and built rival multilateral frameworks (its Global AI Governance Initiative and the World AI Cooperation Organization launched in Shanghai in summer 2026); the authors note that by population alone, roughly one in six assembly seats would belong to someone living in China, framing the proposed assembly as a live test of whether Beijing's rhetoric of inclusive AI governance matches its conduct.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Whether China participates in or boycotts a lottery-based global AI assembly is a concrete, observable signal for assessing the credibility of Beijing's multilateral AI governance rhetoric versus US-led coalitions.
insights.locator: But what about Beijing? The Chinese Communist Party has repeatedly denounced

themes.theme: Precedents and a concrete pacing metric

insights.claim: More than 800 deliberative bodies similar to the proposed assembly have already been convened worldwide according to the OECD, with direct precedents including the 2021 Global Assembly for COP26 (100 people via worldwide lottery), Meta's December 2022 Metaverse Community Forum on Bullying and Harassment (6,300+ people across 32 countries), Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project's 2023 exercise where roughly 1,000 Americans drafted model principles, and Taiwan's March 2024 deliberation on AI and information integrity (200,000 texted, 447 convened online).
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Anthropic already has direct operational experience running a ~1,000-person public deliberation exercise (2023), suggesting it is the frontier lab best positioned to actually adopt this kind of assembly mechanism.
insights.locator: Key parts of this proposal have been tried.

insights.claim: As a concrete, checkable pacing metric, the authors propose that participating labs pilot a transparent safety-research budget equal to 5% to 20% of their compute under published accounting rules, alongside explicit limits on compute used to accelerate capability research, giving evaluators something concrete to verify.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: A published safety-research-to-total-compute ratio (5-20% range) is a candidate KPI investors and watchdogs could push labs to disclose to make 'pacing' commitments auditable rather than rhetorical.
insights.locator: Third, participating labs can make pacing measurable now.

insights.claim: The authors' proposed timeline is that if work starts immediately, a first cohort of the Global Citizens' Assembly on AI could be seated by spring 2027 and deliberating through the rest of 2027.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE AND AUDREY TANG
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete near-term milestone (spring 2027 seating) against which to track whether this governance proposal gains institutional backing or stalls.
insights.quote: If we start today, a first cohort can be seated by spring and deliberating through the rest of 2027.
